1 Executive Summary

This report evaluates the feasibility of designing and implementing a fault tolerant distributed lock service over a cluster of cloud virtual machines connected through a private network. The proposed service coordinates access to shared resources across multiple application instances. A leader orders lock operations, a majority quorum replicates committed state, leases recover locks from failed clients, and monotonically increasing fencing tokens prevent a delayed former owner from modifying a protected resource.

The project is feasible as an academic prototype if the implementation is staged and its claims are limited to tested scenarios. The recommended scope is a three coordinator cluster, named locks, acquire renew release and status operations, durable replicated state, lease expiration, fencing validation, leader failover, monitoring and repeatable fault injection. A production replacement for etcd or Chubby is outside the project scope.

1.1 Main Conditions for Approval

Use an odd sized three node coordinator cluster so that a majority is two nodes.

Treat fencing token enforcement at the protected resource as mandatory, not optional.

Prefer a proven consensus library or a clearly documented simplified replication layer rather than claiming a production grade Raft implementation without evidence.

Define measurable success criteria for mutual exclusion, recovery, failover time and percentile latency.

Stop lock mutations safely whenever a majority quorum cannot be reached.

2 Problem Statement and Scope

2.1 Problem Context

Modern cloud applications commonly run several copies of the same service for scalability and availability. These instances may attempt to update the same record, execute the same scheduled job or control the same shared device. A lock that exists only inside one process cannot coordinate work across different machines. A single central lock server can coordinate them, but it becomes a single point of failure.

Current limitationConsequence
Local in process lockOther virtual machines cannot see the lock and may enter the same critical section.
Single lock serverA server crash makes all lock operations unavailable and may lose ownership state.
Lock without expiryA client crash can leave a resource blocked indefinitely.
Lease without fencingA paused old owner may resume and perform stale work after a new owner is granted the lock.
Unreplicated memory stateRestarting the coordinator may forget current leases and token counters.
Weak failure handlingNetwork partitions can create split brain and conflicting ownership decisions.

2.2 Objectives

Provide mutually exclusive ownership of named resources across multiple clients.

Maintain one ordered and durable view of lock state through leader based quorum replication.

Recover automatically from a single coordinator failure through leader election and state synchronization.

Release abandoned locks through time bounded leases and renewal heartbeats.

Prevent stale owners from producing side effects by issuing strictly increasing fencing tokens.

Support idempotent retries using unique request identifiers.

Expose health metrics logs and fault injection controls for evaluation.

2.3 Scope

Included in the prototypeExcluded or deferred

3 Design Alternatives

Four approaches were evaluated against safety, learning value, implementation effort, failure tolerance and suitability for an academic system design project.

3.1 Option A Single Central Lock Server

One process stores every lock and serves all clients. It is easy to implement and useful as a baseline, but it has a single point of failure and cannot meet the stated fault tolerance objective.

3.2 Option B Database Based Advisory Locks

A relational database or key value store provides conditional writes or advisory locks. This is practical for many applications and reduces implementation effort, but it hides most consensus and recovery mechanisms that the case study is intended to demonstrate.

3.3 Option C Adopt etcd or Consul Directly

A mature coordination platform provides leases, revisions, watch operations and replicated consensus. It is the preferred production choice, but using it without building a visible abstraction offers limited insight into the internal design.

3.4 Option D Custom Educational Coordinator Using Proven Components

Build the client API, lock state machine, leases, fencing, storage, monitoring and failure tests while using a proven consensus library or a deliberately simplified and documented replication module. This preserves the learning objective while reducing the risk of an incorrect consensus implementation.

CriterionA CentralB DatabaseC Existing platformD Proposed prototype
Mutual exclusionGoodGoodExcellentGood when tested
Single node fault tolerancePoorDepends on databaseExcellentGood with quorum
Fencing supportCustomCustomAvailable by revisionExplicit core feature
Learning valueLowMediumMediumVery high
Fit for case studyWeakMediumMediumStrong
Selected alternative Option D is recommended for the academic project. Option C remains the recommendation for an actual production deployment.

4 Proposed System and Architecture

Figure 1 Proposed three node distributed lock service architecture

Clients call one stable endpoint through a load balancer. Requests that change lock state are handled by the current leader. The leader validates the request, appends a command to its durable log, replicates it to followers and commits it only after a two of three majority stores it. The committed command is then applied to the lock state machine.

ComponentResponsibility
Client SDKAdds client and request identifiers, follows leader redirects, renews leases and carries fencing tokens to protected resources.
Load balancerProvides one endpoint and routes traffic only to healthy coordinator nodes.
Leader coordinatorOrders mutations, allocates fencing tokens, replicates commands and returns committed results.
Follower coordinatorsPersist replicated log entries, acknowledge the leader and participate in elections.
Lock state machineMaintains lock owner, lease, expiry, token counter, revision and idempotency records.
Persistent storageStores the write ahead log and periodic snapshots for restart recovery.
Background workersRun heartbeats, election timers, lease expiry, snapshots, log compaction and metrics.
Protected resourceStores the highest accepted fencing token and rejects any request carrying an older token.

4.1 Main Operation Flow

The client sends Acquire with lock name client identity requested lease duration and unique request identifier.

The request reaches the leader directly or is forwarded by a follower.

The leader checks authorization current ownership and request duplication.

If the lock is free the leader creates a log entry containing the next fencing token.

A majority durably acknowledges the entry before it is applied and returned as successful.

The client presents the token to the protected resource and renews the lease before expiry.

Release or expiry is also committed through the replicated log before another owner is granted the lock.

Technical feasibility evaluates whether the required behavior can be built, integrated and tested with available languages, libraries, infrastructure and team skills.

Service languageGoJava or PythonGo offers simple concurrency and efficient network services; team familiarity may decide the final choice.
Client protocolgRPC or RESTCustom TCPREST is easy to demonstrate; gRPC gives clear contracts and streaming watch support.
ConsensusExisting Raft librarySimplified educational replicationA library lowers safety risk; any simplification must be documented and tested.

DeploymentDocker Compose on one machineThree cloud VMsLocal containers support repeatable testing; cloud VMs validate network behavior.

5.2 Component Feasibility

ComponentDifficultyFeasibilityAssessment
Lock API and state modelLowHighStraightforward request validation and deterministic state transitions.
Lease renewal and expiryMediumHighRequires careful timer semantics and replicated expiry commands.
Fencing token generationMediumHighSimple monotonic counter when stored in committed replicated state.
Idempotent retriesMediumHighBounded request result cache keyed by client and request identifier.
WAL snapshot and replayMediumHighEstablished persistence pattern with checksum and crash tests.
Leader follower replicationHighMedium to highFeasible with a tested library and focused integration work.
Automatic leader electionHighMediumMain technical risk; needs deterministic fault tests and time buffer.
Production grade consensusVery highLow for this scheduleExplicitly outside scope unless a mature library supplies it.

5.3 Technical Challenges and Controls

Clock and pause behavior: use conservative lease timing and rely on fencing at the protected resource for final safety.

Split brain: only the majority side may commit changes; the minority must reject or time out mutations.

Crash during persistence: acknowledge only after the required WAL records are durable; validate logs using checksums.

Duplicate and delayed messages: use log term index and idempotency keys so retries do not create extra grants.

State recovery: restore the last complete snapshot and replay valid log entries after its revision.

Technical verdict Feasible for a three node academic prototype. Replication and election are the highest risk items and should use a proven library or a clearly limited design.

6 Operational Feasibility

The system fits applications that require a single active worker or exclusive access to shared state. Adoption requires only a small client library and fencing aware protected operations. The prototype can be started through one scripted command and demonstrated using deterministic client and failure scenarios.

StakeholderInteractionOperational consideration
Application developerAcquire renew release and pass tokensMust handle BUSY timeout and retry without assuming ownership.
Service operatorStart nodes monitor health recover failuresNeeds runbooks for quorum loss storage recovery and membership.
Security administratorManage identities roles and certificatesPeer ports remain private and client permissions are namespace based.
EvaluatorRun workload and fault scenariosNeeds visible metrics repeatable scripts and documented expected results.

6.1 Routine Operations

Monitor leader identity term commit index applied index active leases renewal failures and request latency.

Alert on loss of quorum repeated elections disk errors snapshot failure and high lease expiry rates.

Back up configuration and snapshots and test restoration before the final demonstration.

Use controlled membership changes; do not add or remove several voting nodes simultaneously.

Document startup shutdown partition recovery and complete cluster restart procedures.

Operational verdict High for a supervised prototype and classroom demonstration. A self built service is not recommended for unattended production without mature security monitoring upgrades and incident tooling.

The principal cost is development and testing effort rather than infrastructure. For real production use, adopting a managed or mature open source coordination service is economically preferable because the operational cost of correctness, upgrades and incident response exceeds the cost of the small VM cluster.

Economic verdict Feasible. The prototype can be completed locally at negligible cash cost, while a short cloud validation remains affordable if strict teardown and budget controls are used.

8 Schedule Feasibility

A phased schedule protects the submission by producing a complete basic system before advanced failover work begins. The plan assumes a six to eight week academic implementation window and may be compressed if existing libraries are used.

8.1 Schedule Controls

Freeze the minimum viable scope after Week 1 and move watch streaming dashboards and dynamic membership to stretch goals.

Integrate the client API and fault test harness early rather than leaving demonstration work to the final week.

Maintain a working single node fallback build even while replicated features are under development.

Reserve one week for election bugs recovery bugs and document correction.

Schedule verdict Feasible if the core prototype is prioritized and production grade consensus multi region deployment and advanced membership remain outside the committed scope.

9 Legal Security and Compliance Feasibility

9.1 Licensing and Academic Integrity

Use libraries with compatible open source licenses and retain required copyright and notice files.

Do not copy implementation code from etcd Chubby or other systems without complying with its license and providing attribution.

Cite architecture concepts papers documentation diagrams and externally adapted code.

Keep a dependency register containing package version source and license.

9.2 Security Controls

ThreatControl
Unauthorized lock acquisitionAuthenticate clients and authorize access by lock namespace and operation.
Peer impersonationUse private VPC addressing mutual TLS and a fixed peer identity list.
Replay or duplicate requestRequire unique request identifiers bounded deduplication and lease token checks.
Token disclosure in logsDo not log secrets; redact client credentials and limit operational metadata.
Denial of serviceApply request size limits rate limits lease bounds and per client quotas.
Storage tamperingProtect volumes restrict file permissions and verify WAL and snapshot checksums.

9.3 Data Protection

The prototype should store only coordination metadata and avoid personal or business payloads. Client identifiers should be pseudonymous where possible, logs should have a retention limit, and credentials must be kept outside source control. These controls make legal and privacy requirements manageable for the academic demonstration.

Legal and security verdict Feasible with open source license tracking minimal metadata authenticated access and private encrypted peer communication.

RiskLikelihoodImpactMitigationContingency

10.1 Risk Priority

The two risks that can invalidate the project are conflicting lock grants and stale owner side effects. Therefore, safety invariants and fencing tests must be completed before interface polish, dashboards or performance optimization.

11 Evaluation Plan and Success Criteria

The prototype is successful only when measured evidence supports its safety and recovery claims. Average latency alone is insufficient; percentile latency and interruption during failover must also be reported.

ObjectiveExperimentMetricProposed success criterion
Mutual exclusionTwenty clients compete for one lockSimultaneous committed ownersZero conflicting owners
IdempotencyRepeat one Acquire request 100 timesUnique leases and token incrementsOne logical result and one token allocation
Lease recoveryCrash the owner without releaseTime until another owner is grantedNo grant before expiry and successful grant afterward
Fencing safetyPause old owner then grant a new ownerStale operations acceptedZero stale operations accepted
Leader failoverKill leader under continuous requestsElection and service interruption timeNew leader elected with no conflicting grants
Minority partitionIsolate one coordinatorGrants on minority sideZero mutations committed by the minority
Quorum lossSeparate all three coordinatorsMutation behaviorOperations fail closed or time out
RecoveryRestart follower after many commitsCommit index differenceFollower reaches leader commit index
PerformanceSustained mixed workloadThroughput and p50 p95 p99 latencyReport measured values without unsupported claims

11.1 Evidence to Capture

Coordinator logs showing terms leadership commit indexes and rejected stale operations.

Metrics before during and after each injected failure.

A machine readable test report with pass fail status and timestamps.

Latency distributions throughput and failover interruption rather than only averages.

Screenshots or recordings of the healthy cluster and each controlled failure scenario.

12 Expected Outcomes and Final Recommendation

The expected outcome is a working educational prototype that demonstrates exclusive lock ownership, durable replicated state, time bounded leases, stale owner rejection, single coordinator failure tolerance and safe behavior during partitions. It should include a documented API, deployment scripts, automated correctness tests, fault injection scripts, metrics and a concise demonstration interface or command line client.

Committed outcomeStretch outcome
Named locks and core APIStreaming watch API
Lease renewal and committed expiryDynamic cluster membership
Monotonic fencing tokensMulti availability zone cloud benchmark
WAL snapshot and restart recoveryGraphical monitoring dashboard
Three node quorum and single failure testAdvanced fairness and waiting queues
Repeatable fault test evidenceClient libraries in multiple languages
Final decision GO. The project is technically operationally economically and legally feasible as a controlled academic prototype. Its approval should be tied to phased delivery measurable safety tests mandatory fencing and an explicit statement that the result is not a production replacement for etcd or Chubby.

12.1 Immediate Next Steps

Confirm team details deadline preferred implementation language and whether a consensus library is permitted.

Freeze the API state model safety invariants and Phase 2 acceptance tests.

Implement the single node lock lease and fencing workflow before replication.

Add persistence then integrate the three node quorum cluster.

Run every failure scenario and include only measured claims in the final report.
